text: You timed serial and parallel. Speedup is \({{c1::S(n,p) = \frac{T_{\mathrm{serial} }(n)}{T_{\mathrm{parallel} }(n,p)} }}\). Efficiency is \({{c2::E(n,p) = S(n,p)/p }}\). Linear speedup means \(S = {{c3::p}}\) (so \(E = 1\)).
extra: In practice \(S\) is usually below \(p\) and \(E\) below 1. Mat-vec only got near-linear \(S\) for small \(p\) and large \(n\).

text: For parallel MPI timings, use {{c1::wall clock}} time via \(\mathrm{MPI\_Wtime}\), not CPU time. Wall clock includes {{c2::idle}} time, such as sitting blocked in \(\mathrm{MPI\_Recv}\).
extra: C clock skips idle. Idle can dominate a parallel run, so speedup would be wrong without wall clock.

text: One parallel elapsed time: call {{c1::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Barrier}\)}} so processes start together, time with \(\mathrm{MPI\_Wtime}\), then {{c2::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\)}} with {{c3::\(\mathrm{MPI\_MAX}\)}} on each local elapsed time.
extra: Ideal parallel time is until the last process finishes. Barrier only approximates a simultaneous start.

text: Across repeated identical MPI runs, report the {{c1::minimum}} run-time. OS interaction almost never makes the program {{c2::faster}} than on a quiet system.
extra: Mean or median mix in noise that only slows you. The min approximates the quiet-system time.

text: Usual parallel model: \(T_{\mathrm{parallel} }(n,p) = {{c1::T_{\mathrm{serial} }(n)/p + T_{\mathrm{overhead} } }}\). In MPI that overhead is typically {{c2::communication}}, like Allgather in mat-vec.
extra: Local work falls by about \(p\). Communication can depend on both \(n\) and \(p\).

text: In mat-vec MPI timings, {{c1::communication}} dominates for small \(n\) and large \(p\), so adding processes barely helps. For small \(p\) and large \(n\), local work {{c2::\(T_{\mathrm{serial} }/p\)}} dominates and you get near-linear speedup.
extra: Example: \(n=1024\), \(p=8\) to 16 left run-time unchanged. Worst speedup was 2.4 at \(n=1024\), \(p=16\).

text: Practice: \(T_{\mathrm{serial} }=100\) s, \(T_4=40\) s, \(T_8=25\) s. Speedups are {{c1::2.5 then 4}}. Efficiencies are {{c2::0.625 then 0.5}}. As \(p\) grows, \(E\) {{c3::drops}}.
Roughly, a parallel program is {{c1::scalable}} if you can grow the {{c2::problem size}} fast enough that {{c3::efficiency}} holds as the process count rises.
extra: Mat-vec: fixing \(n\) and raising \(p\) drops \(E\). Doubling both \(n\) and \(p\) (for larger \(p\)) usually holds or raises \(E\).
